tracks.title: Changelogs are marketing
tracks.text: Lesson 02 point 15 — changelogs. A sub-lesson, under nexus. Here's the problem. Every product has a changelog page… and almost every changelog is marketing. Hand-curated. Lagging the real work by days. Written by whoever remembered — so it flatters, and it omits. And nobody can check it… because there's nothing underneath it to check against. [curious] Now the moment agents start committing to your site, that hygiene problem turns into a trust problem. The question stops being is the changelog tidy… and becomes who changed this page, when, and can I verify it. A visitor on an agent-tended site has every right to suspect theater. This lesson is the answer to that suspicion — not a nicer changelog… a changelog you can't fake.

tracks.title: The history endpoint
tracks.text: So here's the definition. The endpoint is called slash underscore changes. And it's an app's real git log, plus its agent's live status… served anonymously by the app itself… and consumed by the very page it describes. Verifiable history, not marketing. The response is one blob with two halves… and each half comes from somewhere honest. First half — changes. That's the literal git log: the last thirty commits, newest first, each one a short sha, a timestamp, an author, and a message — and it comes straight from the git log entries function. Second half — agent. That's the keeper's live heartbeat: active, running, last run, next run — and it comes straight from the keeper status function. [curious] Neither half is composed by hand. Both are read off the running engine, the instant you ask. A thirty-commit cap… a status object… one anonymous request. That's the whole contract.

tracks.title: Anonymous and read-only
tracks.text: Next — anonymous and read-only. This feed does not live where your dashboard lives. A nexus runs two separate planes… and slash underscore changes sits firmly on the anonymous public content plane. Which means it inherits a short list of refusals. First, no auth plug. Second, GET only — you can read it, you cannot write to it. Third, no dock — so no commands, no build, no agents, no secrets. Read by anyone… written by no one. And every response self-identifies, so you always know who's talking: a header that says served by, workbooks runtime… and a marker comment tucked into the HTML. [curious] Now picture how a request finds its app. The browser asks for slash underscore changes with a host header — say, demo dot apps dot example. The engine runs that host through resolve. If it's a registered host, that wins. Otherwise it falls back to the leftmost label — so demo dot apps dot example resolves to the workbook named demo… and out comes the JSON: changes plus agent. But an unknown host? That's a flat four-oh-four — no app for host. There's an authed twin of all this, on the control plane, for the inspector — and its source comment is the canon for this whole lesson: the whole point… is that the changelog is verifiable history… not marketing.

tracks.title: What one change literally is
tracks.text: So what is one change, literally? [curious] There is no changelog database. A change entry is one line of git log… parsed. The engine runs a single formatted log command — git log, with a format string — and it splits each line on tabs into four fields. Read the format aloud and it's almost spoken: percent-h is the short sha. Percent-c-t is the commit time, in unix seconds. Percent-a-n is the author name. And percent-s is the subject — the message. Sha, timestamp, author, message. Newest first. Capped at thirty. And here's why the author can be trusted — commit identity is auth identity. Every commit's name and email are stamped from the authenticated tenant… the email is tenant, at workbooks dot local. You cannot forge an author by typing a different name into a field. The engine stamps it. [curious] And agents never run git themselves — there's no bash outside the sandbox. An agent calls a git tool with only a commit message. The host does the rest: add everything… commit with hooks off… push. The agent supplies intent. The engine supplies identity. That's why the author column is real.

tracks.title: Committed means live
tracks.text: Committed means live. A depth rung — skippable — but it's the line that makes the feed honest in practice. When the host commits for an agent, a successful commit immediately publishes. Inside the same call, the engine mirrors the content folder and the blog folder into the live site directory… before it even pushes. So in this ecosystem, the word committed always implies the word live. And there's a real bug behind that rule. The lander once shipped blog posts that were committed… but returned four-oh-four. Because the run died after the commit, but before a separate publish step ran. Folding publish into commit closed the gap. [curious] Picture the sequence. The agent calls commit, with a message. The git tool tells the host: add everything, then commit with hooks off. The host mirrors content and blog into the site directory. Then it pushes. And it tags the result onto the sha as a literal suffix — pushed… or push failed… or committed, no origin remote. The next poll of the feed shows the new commit. Two guards keep it safe. An auto-generated gitignore means add-everything can never sweep in a signing key. And a safe-directory setting on every git op — without it, a permissions mismatch on the deployed volume once made git refuse everything, and agents wrote to disk for days that never shipped.

tracks.title: Who made this commit
tracks.text: Now the page eats its own feed. Who made this commit? The frontend pulls the feed and classifies every commit by one rule: a commit's type is its message tag. A message shaped tag, colon, something — gets matched against a small table. And a known tag means an agent did it, with a name, a color, and a pill. Walk the table as a list. Add is live green. Rem is purple. Compose is teal. Strategy is a warm orange. Blog and tweet are blue. Audit is amber. And plan, planning, and keeper are a quiet faint gray. Every one of those… is the agent. The matcher looks for a leading tag. If the tag's in the table — that agent, that color. If there's no known tag, but the author's name matches the agent — still the agent, with a fallback tag of work. Everything else… is a human. [curious] Three real commits. First: blog, colon, notes from tending the pricing section. Blog's in the table — so, agent, blue pill. Second: polish the footer, by author waldo. No tag… but the author matches the agent — so, agent, fallback tag work. Third: tighten hero copy, by author shane. No tag, no agent author — human. And because classification lives in the page, you extend it for your own agents just by adding rows. It's a convention… not a constant.

tracks.title: Quiet humans, loud agents
tracks.text: Quiet humans… loud agents. The timeline is opinionated about volume. Consecutive human or system commits collapse — they fold into one foldaway summary that just reads N updates by the team. So a flurry of housekeeping doesn't drown the feed. A single human commit shows inline. But agent commits always render individually — each with its tag pill, and its short sha linked to the public commit on the mirror. The choice is deliberate. Agents narrate loudly, because their work is the thing under scrutiny. Humans stay quiet by default. So those three commits from before: the blog commit stands alone as an agent line… and the three human commits fold into one summary — three updates by the team. [curious] And one discipline keeps the readouts honest. There is one poller. The hero ticker does not open a second connection — it subscribes to the same feed, and reuses the engine's own classify function, so the ticker can't drift from the panel. Picture it: the feed polls, checks each new sha against a seen set. New agent commit — render it individually, pill and sha. New human commit — fold it into the team summary. Meanwhile the ticker rides the very same feed. Two readouts… one truth. There's one extra flourish — a fresh add commit makes the page type its new section in, character by character, with a green wash. But the source is explicit: that's cosmetic streaming over a plain swap. It is not a real shared-document merge.

tracks.title: Narrating the run
tracks.text: Narrating the run — another depth rung, skippable. The changes feed tells you what already happened. Its sibling, slash underscore activity, narrates what's happening right now — same public plane, same refusals. It returns the keeper's status, plus the tail of the steps file — the agent's step telemetry in the repo — plus one cosmetic narration line. The steps get slimmed for the public. Each event becomes four things: the tool, the timestamp, the agent, and a target — whichever path, command, pipeline, query, or url the step had — sliced to a hundred and twenty characters. [curious] Picture the round trip. The page asks for slash underscore activity. The endpoint reads the keeper's status — from fast in-memory storage, never a blocking call. It tails the steps file and slims each line. And it asks a tiny side model for a caption — but only if someone's actually watching. Back comes agent, steps, and a thought. The thought is that side model captioning the feed in eight words or fewer. Purely cosmetic. Fully decoupled from the agent. Lazy, debounced on a twenty-second timer, cached per agent, and degrading to the last cached line on failure. And when the agent's idle, the thought falls back to the newest daydream the keeper left behind. It's a caption… not chain-of-thought. And the page never pretends otherwise.

tracks.title: Thinking, honestly
tracks.text: Thinking, honestly. This is the section that earns the lesson. A watch-the-agent-work feed is exactly where products lie — they animate a fake cursor and call it transparency. This one refuses… by deriving its claims from the data, instead of performing them. The keystone is a freshness window. The follow loop polls activity every two and a half seconds. And the freshness constant is twenty-five thousand milliseconds. A step older than twenty-five seconds means the page says — thinking. Because that's what the model is actually doing between tool calls. The source comment is the whole thesis: the model generating between tool calls is most of an agent's wall time… and ninety percent real beats a hundred percent theatrical. [curious] It's one little state machine, three places. Picture it. A fresh step whose target is on this page — that's on-page. A fresh step whose target is somewhere else — off-page. And no step at all for twenty-five seconds — thinking. A fresh step lands… and it snaps back to on-page. That's the entire machine. Now, privacy, on the same feed. A target is never shown raw if it's a private API — it's mapped to a label. Search providers become checking search data. Model hosts become thinking. The posting endpoint becomes posting an update. GitHub becomes reading the repo. Anything else that looks like an api host… becomes simply, working. So a step pointed at a model API renders one word — thinking. Never the url. Never the args. One worked window, end to end. A real step on disk: tool, vfs write… agent, waldo… path, content slash sections slash zero-seven pricing. The feed slims that to tool, timestamp, agent, and target. The page resolves the path to the pricing element… and parks the cursor in a typing descent. Twenty-five seconds later, no fresh step — the portal flips to thinking. True… not theatrical.

tracks.title: What it isn't
tracks.text: What it isn't — the honesty section. The good version of a feature tells you its own edges. So here they are. First — thirty commits. The feed is hard-capped. It's a recent-history window, not a full archive. Second — polling, not push. The page refreshes every fifteen to twenty seconds, follow-mode every two and a half. No websockets. Live means polled often, not instant. Third — classification is convention. Who-did-what is inferred from a message tag and an author name. Not signed. Not cryptographic. A human who types blog colon… renders as the agent. The author column is trustworthy. The type pill is a helpful guess. Fourth — the thought is cosmetic. A side model's caption — not the agent's real reasoning. Fifth — the steps file is editable today. It's plain text in the repo. Tamper-evident provenance is the frontier the ledger lesson takes up — and this page doesn't claim signing it doesn't have. [curious] And last — it needs a keeper. The agent half of the feed is the keeper's status. No keeper running… no agent block. The changes half still works. The live narration just goes quiet.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I get this for free when I publish? Yes. It's the public plane, plus your repo — nothing to build. Publish on a nexus, and the changes endpoint already answers on its host. Can visitors write anything through it? No. GET only, no auth, no dock. Read by anyone, written by no one. Can I change the tags and colors? Yes — classification is page-side. The type map lives in the frontend… so you add rows for your own agents and pick their colors. Why does my human teammate show as the agent? Because they used an agent tag. A commit shaped blog colon matches the table regardless of author. Drop the prefix, and the human renders as a human. And where's the proof a commit is real? The sha. Every agent commit links to the public mirror, where you read the diff yourself — the same bytes the page previews. The write rail behind it is the gitops lesson. And commit identity is auth identity — stamped by the host, not typed by the committer.

tracks.title: Back up to nexus
tracks.text: So that's changelogs. Not a page someone writes — the repo… told live. An anonymous, read-only feed of your real git log, plus your agent's heartbeat, consumed by the very page it describes — classified, collapsed, and narrated honestly. The whole point being that it's verifiable history, not marketing. [curious] If you want the surfaces underneath it… the way up is short. This is a sub-lesson under nexus — the engine that serves the feed. From there, planes covers the two HTTP surfaces it lives on… gitops covers the write rail that commits and publishes… and keepers covers where that agent block comes from. Head back up to nexus… and pick your next thread.
